What is covered

Cabinet refinishing, in full

  • Doors and drawer fronts removed, numbered and worked off site or in a controlled space
  • Degreasing, which is the step that decides whether the finish sticks
  • Sanding, filling and a bonding primer made for cabinets
  • Sprayed finish coats, not brush marks
  • Hardware refitted, or new hardware fitted if you are changing it
  • Boxes and face frames done in place

How the job runs

The order it happens in

  1. Look at the boxes firstIf the carcasses are sound, refinishing makes sense. If they are falling apart or the layout is wrong, you are better off being told that than being sold a finish on top of a bad box.
  2. Doors off and labeledEvery door and drawer front comes off and gets numbered so it goes back exactly where it came from. Hinges and hardware bagged with it.
  3. Degrease, then sandA kitchen has years of cooking film on it. Skipping the degreasing is the single most common reason a cabinet job peels within a year.
  4. Bonding primerCabinets need a primer built to stick to a finished factory surface. Wall primer is not it.
  5. Spray the finishSprayed, so there is no brush texture on a surface your hand touches every day.
  6. Cure, then rehangThe finish needs time before it is handled. Rushing this is how fingerprints end up permanent.

What moves the number

Why two quotes for the same room can look nothing alike

No price is published here, because a real number needs somebody to stand in the room first. What can be published is what actually drives it, so you can read any quote you get and know what you are looking at.

  1. How many doors and drawersCabinets are counted, not measured by kitchen. Two kitchens of the same size can have very different door counts.
  2. What they are made ofSolid wood, veneer, thermofoil and laminate all take different preparation and not all of them take paint well. This gets checked before it is quoted.
  3. How greasy they areDegreasing is real labor and it varies enormously between kitchens.
  4. Inside the boxes or notDoing the interiors is a meaningful addition. Most people do not need it. It should be your decision, made with the number in front of you.
  5. Whether you are changing hardwareNew handles often mean new holes, filled old holes, and that has to happen before the finish goes on.

Ask every contractor the same three questions

What preparation is included. How many coats. What happens to the price if the preparation turns out to be worse than it looks. The answers, more than the total, are what tell you which quote is real.

Questions

About cabinet refinishing

Is painting cabinets actually worth it, or should I replace them?

It depends entirely on the boxes. If the carcasses are solid, the doors are not delaminating and you are happy with the layout, refinishing changes the look of the room for a fraction of a replacement. If the boxes are shot or the layout is wrong, paint will not fix that and you should be told so.

How long does it take?

It is a multi-day job, not an afternoon. Doors come off, get prepped, get finished and then have to cure before they are handled. You get a realistic day count at the walk-through, including how long the kitchen is partly out of action.

Will it chip?

A cabinet finish lives or dies on preparation. Degreased, sanded, primed with a bonding primer and sprayed, it holds up to daily use. Painted over grease with wall paint, it will not last a year. That difference is most of the price difference between quotes.

Can you spray, or is it brushed?

Sprayed. On a surface you touch every day, brush texture is the first thing you notice and the last thing you stop noticing.

Can you do bathroom vanities too?

Yes, same process, smaller job. It is often worth adding to a kitchen job while the equipment is already set up.
